title: Waiting for a six
hook: A six takes 6 rolls on average. Are you as likely to need more than 6 as fewer?

knows: a fair die shows a six 1 time in 6
doesNotKnow: that the average wait and the typical wait differ for a first success
that a long right tail pulls the average up

misconception: If the average wait for a six is 6 rolls, you are as likely to wait more than 6 rolls as fewer.
objective: The learner can explain that only about a third of players need more than 6 rolls ((5/6)^6 = 33%), half are done by roll 4, and a few very long waits pull the average up to 6.
keyState: Histogram of 1,000 players rolled; marker at 6 (338 beyond, 34%) and at 4 (491 beyond: half done by roll 4).

claims.text: Rolling a fair die until the first six takes 6 rolls on average.
The chance of needing more than 6 rolls is (5/6)^6, about 33%.
claims.source: P(no six in 6 rolls) = (5/6)^6 = 0.3349 (exactMoreThan() in src/demos/probability/average-wait-six-rolls/model.ts). Options 10% / 33% / 50%.

claims.text: On the stage, 338 of 1,000 players (34%) needed more than 6 rolls, 491 needed more than 4 (so half were done by roll 4), and the average was 5.9 rolls; 11 players needed 25 rolls or more.
claims.source: waits() in model.ts, mulberry32 seed 6, untuned (the first seed tried); longest wait 59. Over seeds 1-1000: average middle 95% 5.68-6.34 (median 6.00); more than 6: 307-364 (median 335); half done by roll 4 in the median seed (range 4-5).

claims.text: Exactly, half the players are done by roll 4: the chance of a six within 4 rolls is 52%, within 3 only 42%.
claims.source: 1 - (5/6)^4 = 0.518; 1 - (5/6)^3 = 0.421. Not quoted verbatim on stage; supports 'Half were done by roll 4' in the reveal alongside c3.

claims.text: Most players finish early but a few wait very long, and those long waits pull the average above what a typical player sees.
claims.source: The geometric distribution is right-skewed: median 4 < mean 6 (c1, c4).

recall.question: A machine fails on average once every 10 days, at random. On a given restart, is it more likely to fail before day 10 or after?
recall.why: Random waiting times bunch up early with a long tail of long waits. The chance of lasting past the average is about (1 - 1/10)^10 = 35%, so failing before day 10 is more likely.
